conventional_description: In Western medicine, spider veins (telangiectasias) are small, widened blood vessels that appear near the surface of the skin, looking like thin red or purple lines or web-like patterns. They can occur anywhere on the body but are most common on the face and legs. Common causes include genetics, sun damage, aging, hormonal changes like pregnancy or menopause, rosacea, and sometimes underlying liver disease. Diagnosis is usually made by visual inspection; no special tests are needed unless a deeper medical condition is suspected.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment focuses on cosmetic removal or camouflaging the veins. Options include laser therapy, intense pulsed light (IPL), sclerotherapy (injecting a solution to close the vein), and electrocautery. Topical creams may temporarily reduce redness but don't eliminate the vessels. Sun protection is often advised to prevent worsening.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, spider veins are understood as a problem of blood and vessel health, closely tied to the Liver's role of ensuring smooth Qi and Blood flow throughout the body. When emotional stress, frustration, or hormonal shifts cause Liver Qi to stagnate, blood flow becomes sluggish and can pool in the small vessels under the skin, creating the dark, web-like patterns. Over time, this stagnation can generate heat, which agitates the blood and dilates the vessels further, making them more visible.
Blood heat is a key factor in many spider veins, especially when they appear bright red. Heat can arise from internal imbalances like Liver Fire, Damp-Heat, or Yin deficiency, and it pushes blood outward with force, weakening the delicate capillary walls. This creates the central red dot with radiating branches that gives spider veins their name. The combination of stasis and heat is extremely common - blood that isn't moving smoothly overheats and expands, much like a slow-moving river that warms in the sun.
The Spleen and Kidneys also play important roles. The Spleen governs the integrity of the vessel walls and produces the Qi that holds blood inside the vessels. When Spleen Qi is weak, the vessels become fragile and blood can seep or dilate. Kidney Yin deficiency, often from chronic stress or aging, allows an empty, restless heat to rise and disturb the blood, causing fragile, transient spider veins especially on the face and chest. This is why spider veins can appear in so many different contexts - the same visible sign can stem from entirely different internal roots.
This is why TCM doesn't see spider veins as one condition with one treatment. A person with dark, purplish veins and rib-side pain has Liver Blood Stagnation. Someone with bright red veins, a bitter taste in the mouth, and a thick tongue coating has Damp-Heat. Another person with night sweats and hot palms has Kidney Yin deficiency. Each pattern requires a fundamentally different strategy, even though the skin looks similar.
classical_quote: 「血痣者，乃肝经怒火郁结，其形初起色红如痣，渐大如豆，揩之血流。」
classical_translation: "Blood moles arise from the stagnation of anger in the Liver channel. Initially they appear red like a mole, gradually enlarge to the size of a bean, and bleed when rubbed."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by looking at the whole person, not just the spider veins. They will ask about the color, location, and any sensations around the spots, then explore what else is happening in your body - your digestion, emotions, energy level, and any other skin changes. The tongue’s color, coating, and shape, along with the pulse’s quality, are the crucial clues that reveal which internal imbalance is driving the visible veins.
When Blood Stagnation with Heat is the main pattern, the spider veins tend to be bright red and the skin may feel warm. The tongue often appears dark purple with small purple spots, and the pulse feels deep and hesitant or wiry. You might also notice thirst, constipation, or a sensation of heat in the body. This pattern is a direct picture of blood that is both stuck and overheated, pushing outward against the vessel walls.
Liver Blood Stagnation shows up when emotional stress or hormonal shifts have tied the liver’s smooth flow into knots. The spider veins often appear on the trunk or face, and you may feel distension or discomfort under the ribs, irritability, or irregular periods. The tongue is usually dark or purplish with a thin white or slightly yellow coating, and the pulse feels wiry, like a taut guitar string, signaling that Qi and blood are not moving freely.
In Heat in the Blood, the red spider veins are accompanied by other signs of heat, such as a red face, a feeling of being too warm, nosebleeds, or heavy menstrual bleeding. The tongue is red with a yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and slippery. This pattern often flares up during pregnancy, with spicy foods, or when internal heat is already stirring, agitating the blood and dilating the tiny vessels.
Damp-Heat in the Liver combines the heaviness of dampness with the flaring of heat. The tongue has a thick, greasy yellow coating and the pulse is slippery and rapid or wiry. You might notice a bitter taste in the mouth, a heavy feeling in the body, and perhaps a yellowish tint to the eyes or skin. A history of rich food, alcohol, or chronic liver strain often lies behind this pattern, and the skin changes are just one part of a wider picture of sluggish, overheated circulation.
When Kidney Yin Deficiency with Empty-Heat Blazing is the root, the spider veins tend to be finer and appear alongside signs of dryness and false heat - night sweats, a dry mouth at night, a malar flush across the cheeks, and a tongue that is red with little or no coating. The pulse is thin and rapid. This pattern is more common in chronic illness or aging, where the body’s cooling, nourishing reserves have been depleted, allowing empty heat to rise and disturb the blood.
Spleen Deficiency with Dampness produces spider veins against a backdrop of fatigue, pale complexion, bloating, and loose stools. The tongue is pale and puffy with a white, greasy coating, and the pulse is weak and slippery. Because the spleen fails to transform fluids and generate healthy blood, dampness accumulates and the vessels become fragile, making them more likely to show through the skin.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When blood flow becomes sluggish or stuck, it creates a pool of stagnant blood in the small vessels. At the same time, internal heat agitates the blood, pushing it outward and dilating the capillaries. This combination of stasis and heat produces the characteristic red, spider-like lesion with a central pulsating point and radiating legs.
The heat gives the spot its bright red color, while the stagnation causes the vessel to remain permanently widened. This is why spider veins often appear in areas where circulation is naturally slower and why they may darken over time as the stasis deepens.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: reddish-purple body with stasis spots, distended sublingual veins, thin dry yellow coat. Pulse: choppy (涩 sè) and rapid (数 shuò), often wiry (弦 xián) at the left Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Heat and stagnation are the twin drivers of this pattern. Alcohol, spicy food, and hot weather pour more heat into the blood, making vessels dilate further and stasis worse. Emotional stress constrains Liver Qi, which directly leads to blood stasis. Rest, cooling foods, and cold compresses pull heat out of the blood, while gentle movement and stress relief keep Qi and blood moving, preventing the pooling that creates visible veins.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle:
Favor cooling, blood-nourishing foods like cucumber, celery, mung beans, and dark leafy greens. Avoid alcohol, spicy foods, and excessive red meat, which can add heat and thicken the blood.
Gentle daily movement such as walking or yoga helps keep blood flowing smoothly. Manage stress with regular relaxation practices, as emotional tension worsens both stasis and heat.

patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yin is the body's deepest cooling reserve. When it becomes depleted through chronic illness, aging, or overwork, it can no longer anchor the body's warm Yang energy. This allows a restless, empty heat to rise upward and agitate the blood, causing tiny surface vessels to dilate and become fragile. The result is the red, spider-like veins that appear on the skin alongside other signs of deep yin deficiency.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, dry body with little or no coating, possible cracks. Pulse: fine (xi) and rapid (shu), especially weak at the rear (chi) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Empty heat arises because yin is too weak to anchor yang. Anything that further depletes yin - like overwork, late nights, or excessive sexual activity - worsens the condition by deepening the deficit. Heating foods and alcohol directly add heat, which flares upward and agitates the blood vessels. Rest, cooling foods, and yin-nourishing practices help replenish the body's cooling capacity, allowing the empty heat to subside and the fragile capillaries to stabilize.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and hot-natured foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which can flare empty heat. Instead, eat cooling, moistening foods like pear, black sesame, kidney beans, and goji berries. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork, especially staying up late, which depletes yin further. Gentle activities like restorative yoga or walking support yin without overheating the body.

faqs.question: Will acupuncture make my spider veins disappear?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture alone rarely makes existing veins vanish instantly, but it plays a crucial role in correcting the internal imbalance that causes them. By moving Qi and blood, clearing heat, and strengthening the organs, regular acupuncture sessions can help prevent new veins and gradually reduce the prominence of existing ones. Many practitioners also use local points around the veins to improve circulation in the area, which supports the fading process.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Yes, dietary adjustments are an important part of treatment because certain foods can fuel the internal heat or dampness that drives spider veins. In general, it's best to avoid alcohol, spicy foods, greasy or fried foods, and excessive sugar. Instead, focus on cooling, blood-nourishing foods like leafy greens, cucumber, celery, and mung beans. Your practitioner may give more specific advice based on your pattern - for example, someone with Spleen deficiency will need warm, cooked meals, while someone with Damp-Heat may need to avoid dairy and rich foods.

faqs.question: Can TCM help if my spider veins are from sun damage or aging?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. While sun damage and aging are external triggers, TCM views them as factors that deplete the body's Yin and Blood, making the vessels more fragile and prone to dilation. By nourishing Yin, strengthening Blood, and clearing any resulting heat, TCM can address the susceptibility that allows these veins to form. Treatment focuses on rebuilding your skin's resilience from the inside out, which can reduce both existing and future spider veins.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with laser treatments?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM can be safely used alongside laser or light-based therapies. In fact, combining the two can be powerful - laser treats the visible veins, while herbs and acupuncture work to correct the underlying imbalance and prevent recurrence. Just be sure to inform both your dermatologist and your TCM practitioner about all treatments you are receiving. If you are taking blood-moving herbs, your dermatologist should know, as they can sometimes increase skin sensitivity or bruising risk after procedures.

faqs.question: How long before I see results?
faqs.answer: The first changes are usually internal - you may notice less bloating, better digestion, more stable moods, or a reduction in feelings of heat within 4-6 weeks. New spider veins tend to stop appearing around this time. The fading of existing veins is slower and more gradual, often taking 3-6 months of consistent treatment. Long-standing deficiency patterns may require longer, but even in those cases, many people feel significantly better in their overall health before the veins fully fade.

faqs.question: What does the color of my spider veins tell the practitioner?
faqs.answer: Color is a valuable clue. Bright red veins usually point to heat in the blood, while dark purple or bluish veins suggest blood stasis. If the veins are pale and associated with fatigue and pale skin, blood deficiency may be at the root. Your practitioner will combine this observation with your tongue, pulse, and other symptoms to pinpoint the exact pattern.

faqs.question: Are there any side effects from the herbs?
faqs.answer: Herbal formulas are prescribed specifically for your pattern and are generally well tolerated. Some blood-moving herbs may cause slightly looser stools or mild digestive changes initially, which usually resolve quickly. It's important to inform your practitioner of any medications you take, especially blood thinners, as herbs like Dang Gui and Chuan Xiong can interact with them. Your practitioner will adjust the formula if you experience any discomfort.

research.title: Clinical application progress of promoting blood circulation and removing blood stasis in TCM treatment of liver cirrhosis
research.description: This review analyzed multiple Chinese clinical studies using blood-activating formulas like Xue Fu Zhu Yu Tang in patients with liver cirrhosis. It reported that spider nevi, along with other signs of portal hypertension, showed improvement in 60-80% of cases after treatment, suggesting that moving blood and resolving stasis can reduce the appearance of spider veins by improving liver microcirculation.
